By the dawn,
and the ten nights,
and the even and the odd,
and the night when it passes.

Is there not in this an oath for one of understanding?

Wait, the passage given is only the commentary, not the verse text. Here is the translation of the commentary as it stands:

In the opening of this surah, for the purpose of swearing an oath, such scenes and creatures have been chosen as are familiar scenes to human beings, possess a delicate spirit, and are clear and transparent. "Al-Fajr" (the dawn) is a time at which life breathes in a most pleasant mood. In feelings of great joy, smiling, love and fresh attachment, this entire universe stretches itself awake. These breaths of dawn are, as it were, the breaths of supplication to God. And at the time of dawn everything appears open and unfolded; it seems as though buds are blossoming out of joy.

"And by the ten nights" (89:2). The Qur'an leaves these ten nights unspecified. Commentaries contain sayings and reports about their identity: some say they are the ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah, some say the ten nights of Muharram, and some mention the ten nights of Ramadan. In my view, they should be left general and unrestricted as they are, and this is more pleasing. These ten nights, which only Allah knows, and which hold a particular station and significance with Allah, are illuminated in the context of the discourse in such a way that perhaps they are a living entity and nights with a soul, just as a living being is a creature with a soul. These nights love us, and we love them, in the mirror of this Qur'anic expression.

"By the dawn, and by the even and the odd," (89:3) — the quoted verse rendered plainly. In this familiar and beloved atmosphere of the morning, and in the ten honoured nights, the even (shaf') and the odd (watr) are the very spirit of prayer. The words of the noble hadith are: "In prayer there is shaf' and there is watr" (Tirmidhi). The atmosphere that prevails in these verses points to this meaning as more appropriate. The fitting meaning is the union of the worshipping soul with the spirit of this all-encompassing universe, just as a worshipping soul attains union with the spirit during the ten nights beloved of Allah, and then these nights and this bright emergence of dawn all join together.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 89, verse 4:

﴿And by the night when it passes away.﴾ Is this a night, or is it a living creature that moves about in this universe? It is as though it were a lovesick lover wandering through the nights, or a traveller journeying by night toward a distant destination. What a beautiful manner of expression! How familiar is the scene! How pleasant is the melody of the words. In "al-Fajr," "layali 'ashr" and "ash-shaf'i wal-witr," the harmony of words, melody and meaning is worth seeing. These are not mere words and phrases, but the pleasant and warm breaths of the dawn's appearance, fragrant sounds, loving conversations upon the grieving heart, or the subtle whisperings of the soul, or the signs and moments of the awakening of the human conscience.

Look at the beauty: a beauty full of loving whispers, a free poetic beauty, which does not even equal its trace. This is a miraculously created beauty, and it is also composed of truths together with grace and loveliness.

For this reason, immediately after these oaths, it is said:

Is there, in that, an oath for one of understanding? This is a rhetorical question, the answer to which is: Indeed, in it there is an oath for a person of intellect. Yes, in it there is reassurance and consolation for every person of understanding and reason. This interrogative style has been adopted for this affirmation because it is more fitting with the gentle, whispering manner found in these oaths.

Here, the matter upon which the oath is sworn has been wrapped up within the context of the speech, so that curiosity remains alive and the subsequent discourse explains it. The subsequent theme is that of rebellion, corruption, oppression, and transgression of limits, and of the conduct of the Hand of Divine Power toward such people: that Allah certainly takes vengeance upon such people, and it is upon this that Allah swears. And the oath is sworn in a manner that is extremely gentle, allusive, and concise.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 89, verses 6–8:

The interrogative form, in this kind of context, is striking and draws the listeners' attention more strongly. Although the address is at first to the Prophet (ﷺ), it afterwards applies to every person who is capable of taking a lesson from the cautionary accounts of these peoples. At the time these verses were revealed, the stories of these peoples were well known among those being addressed. The ancient remains that still survive in this region, and the tales that are still on everyone's lips, also show that the Arabs knew these peoples well. Here the subject of the verb has been brought as "your Lord" (Rabbuka). In this there is a source of reassurance for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and for the handful of Muslims of that time. At that time the Muslims of Makkah were suffering oppression at the hands of the rebellious among the Quraysh, and these people were standing in the way against them on every front. This manner of expression produces comfort and affection in their hearts.

In these brief verses, Allah has pointed to the accounts of the leading tyrants of human history. Among them is the well-known people of ʿĀd, Iram, who are also called ʿĀd the First (ʿĀd al-Ūlā). They were among those Arabs who were pure Arabs in the early ages (al-ʿĀribah), or among those Arabs whose lineage has been extinct (al-Bā'idah). These people lived in al-Ahqāf; al-Ahqāf refers to sand dunes. Their remains still exist between Yemen and Hadramawt in southern Arabia. They were nomadic people and lived in tents that stood on pillars. The Holy Qur'an has explicitly stated that they were very strong and possessed the power of severe seizure. In their time they were the most powerful people and were distinguished among the nations.

﴿The likes of which were not created in the lands﴾ (89:8): meaning, up to that time.

﴿Those who transgressed greatly in the lands, and caused much corruption therein﴾ [Al-Fajr 89:11-12]. [Original reads: "الذین ... الفساد (12:89)"]

These were the people who committed great rebellion in the lands of the world and spread corruption in them. Corruption naturally follows rebellion, because rebellion ruins the rebellious person. Likewise, those who fall victim to rebellion and oppression also become afflicted with corruption. A moral decay arises within them. After this, every aspect of collective life comes under the grip of corruption, and life departs from its healthy, constructive and pure path and falls onto paths that are contrary to the responsibility of man as khalifatullah fil-ard (vicegerent of Allah on earth).

Because of tyranny and rebellion, the common people become enslaved and humiliated, and a hidden hatred and envy arise within them. They keep their anger and envy suppressed in their hearts at all times. From the personalities of such people, self-respect and the lofty human consciousness are erased, and creative capacity is extinguished among them. It is worth noting that a free atmosphere is essential for the creative process. And a society that a dictator keeps in humiliation becomes putrid, and becomes a rotting society. In it, people live a degraded life, like insects and worms. At most, they become addicted to base habits and debauchery. Their faculties of intellect and wisdom grow dull, and crimes arise among such people in every field of life. Their faculties of intellect and wisdom grow dull, and crimes arise among such people in every field of life. In such people, lofty qualities such as self-respect, courage, high aspirations and far-sightedness are destroyed, and this is a very great corruption.

Dictators and tyrants always uproot lofty values and sound thinking from their foundations. Therefore, lofty values and sound thinking pose a threat to their false power. Hence tyrants always devise corrupt values for people and establish depraved standards in societies, and by spreading wrong ideas and concepts they make them appear attractive, so that people accept their aggression, domination and tyranny, and regard it as a popular, accepted and prevailing ideology. And this is the great corruption beyond which there is no greater corruption. And when such people spread all-encompassing corruption across the earth, the purification of the earth becomes necessary.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 89, verse 13:

﴿Then your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord is in ambush.﴾ (14:89) Your Lord is in ambush, and He is recording their deeds. When their corruption exceeds all bounds, the whip of Allah begins to strike, and the process of the punishment of Allah descending upon them in this very world begins. The "scourge of punishment" here refers to the severity and sting of the punishment. The meaning is that the punishment of Allah is very widespread and all-encompassing, and it is poured upon these rebels from every side, with pain, sting and depth, and it overwhelms those rebels who, through their insolence, had filled the earth with corruption.

When the believers and the callers to the truth (dāʿiyān-i-ḥaqq) who have to deal with such oppressors and rebels see the end of these tyrants and dictators, the blessings of tranquility descend upon their hearts, wherever and in whatever time and place they may be. Then, the words that the Qur'an has used...

Verily your Lord is ever watchful (14:89). That is, your Lord is present and helpful. He sees, and nothing escapes His sight. He is observing, and nothing is hidden from His gaze. Therefore the believers should be at peace; their troubles will be removed, because the Lord is watching, and He Himself will deal with evil and corruption, and will also punish in the Hereafter.

We see that in this world the Islamic call is supported in extraordinary ways; the method of the People of the Ditch (ashab al-ukhdud) does not appear everywhere. In accordance with this method the Qur'an trains those who work for the religion in this manner, and in different circumstances and different environments their training and support continue in different ways, and there remains a source of tranquillity for the callers to truth. The people of faith hold two expectations, and after their struggle they entrust the outcome and the decision to the will of Allah, for He is watching.

Your Lord lies in ambush. He is present and watching, the reckoning is being prepared, and He will give recompense on the basis of a perfectly accurate record of deeds, in which there is no error and no injustice, and which is not merely based on outward circumstances as worldly reckoning is; rather there all matters will be decided according to realities. As for man, in this world his assessments also go wrong, his estimates also go wrong, and in testimony too he judges by appearances, unless he makes a decision in accordance with the Shari'ah of Allah and thinks according to the Islamic conception of life.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 89, verses 15–16:

فاما الاانسان ............................ اھانن

This is the human being's way of thinking about the circumstances through which he passes. At times he is rich, at times poor; sometimes ease (firakhi) is granted to him and sometimes constraint (tangi). Sometimes Allah tests him with blessings and honours, and sometimes his test comes through status and wealth. But he does not understand that this is a trial, in which success earns a reward. Rather, his thinking is that from the ease of wealth and property and from honour and status he draws the conclusion that he deserves that rank and standing in the sight of Allah, and that this wealth and this honour are proof that he is accepted by Allah. Because of this misunderstanding, he regards the trial as a reward and the examination as a result. He also measures honour and rank in the sight of Allah by the honour and rank of this world. In the same way, if such a person becomes poor, he thinks that perhaps he has been punished. He regards the trial as a punishment. And if Allah has reduced his provision, he considers this a punishment and a humiliation. His thinking is that, were it not for this humiliating treatment, Allah would not have made him poor.

In both states, the person who thinks this way is in error. Just as his thinking is wrong, his assessment is also wrong. The real matter is that the constraint of provision is a trial, and the abundance of provision is also a trial. Abundance is a trial in that it is seen whether he gives thanks for it or uses wealth as a means of injustice and rebellion; and in the case of constraint, it is seen whether he is patient or displays bad temper. In both circumstances, reward and punishment will follow according to his response. Worldly wealth and worldly poverty are, in themselves, neither a reward nor a punishment. The servants of Allah are not weighed by their wealth. Neither the granting nor the withholding of blessings in this world is a sign of Allah's pleasure or of His displeasure. Allah gives to the righteous and gives to the wicked; He withholds from the righteous and He also gives to them.

When a human heart is empty of faith, it cannot understand the wisdom behind Allah's giving or withholding, and it does not grasp the standards of good and bad that Allah has established. But when a heart is filled with faith, that person becomes one who has attained nearness to God, and he knows what carries weight in the balance of Allah. For such a person, the low-value gains of this world become light, and he knows that a reward follows from the trial. So he works for the Hereafter in both states, abundance and constraint, and is content with the decree of Allah in both. Even without the outward glitter of worldly life, he understands the values that carry weight with Allah, and the weightless values of this world appear worthless to him.

The direct addressees of the Qur'an were the people of Makkah. Such people are found in every society. Their fault is that they cannot conceive of a wider and greater world beyond this one. These were people who held the view about the constraint and abundance of provision, and about Allah, that has been mentioned above. In keeping with this thinking, they determined the worth of people on this earth. In short, for them wealth and status were everything; beyond that, they had no criterion. This is why they chased wealth and went to excess in their love of property. Because of this, they were extremely greedy and held hopes of gain from everyone in their hearts, and due to this disposition they became very avaricious. Thus Allah here opens up the inner state of these people and tells us that this greed for wealth which is deeply rooted in their hearts exists because their thinking about wealth and property is mistaken. They do not understand that wealth is not only a blessing but also a trial. Likewise, poverty is not merely a calamity but also a trial.

Nay, but... [the Qur'anic quotation from 89:17–18 is elided in the source as "کلا بل ... حباجما"; the passage itself begins below]

The matter is not as a man devoid of faith imagines it to be: that merely because someone has been granted abundant provision, this is a sign of honour in the sight of Allah. Nor does straitened provision prove that such a person has no worth with Allah or that Allah has abandoned him. The reality is that you do not fulfil the right of wealth and do not extract the dues owed from your wealth. You do not even provide for the orphan, who has been deprived of his parents, guardians and protectors. Likewise, you make no arrangement for the economic support of the needy within society. The meaning of miskin (the needy) is one who is still, who sits in quietness and does not roam about asking people. Here it is said that you do not urge others to feed the orphans and the needy, that is, to provide for their material needs. This indicates that in an Islamic system there is a general movement for the support of the needy: people compete with one another for the good of the common folk and urge one another to it. Support of the needy is a distinguishing feature of Islam.

You understand the concept of trial (ibtila'), yet you do not wish to succeed in that trial, whereas the path to success in that trial is that you honour the orphan, enjoin and exhort one another that orphans be fed. Rather, you adopt the opposite course. You devour the entire inheritance with extreme greed, and you love wealth with an immoderate love that knows no limit. In matters of wealth there is no self-respect or dignity among you. And you neither honour the needy nor attend to their need.

As we have already given details earlier, in Makkah the situation was such that people were extremely greedy and ran like dogs after their interests, gathering wealth by every means, which gave rise to miserliness and hardheartedness in their hearts. Because orphans were helpless, their property was devoured. Especially the property of orphan women. Then they would deprive them of inheritance, as we have given details at several places. Apart from these stratagems, the people of Makkah were also engaged day and night in accumulating wealth through usurious dealings. It is worth noting here that the worship of wealth is the characteristic of every jahiliyyah (age of ignorance), wherever and whenever it may be.

In these verses not only is their stance well described, but it is also condemned, and this situation is made intolerable with great severity, and for this the word "kalla" (certainly not) is used, meaning: it cannot be so at all, it should not be so at all. The manner of expression of the verses, their forceful interpretation and the tremendous tone of the words also convey the condemnation of this state of affairs. Reflect once more.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 89, verses 19–20:

"And you devour the inheritance, devouring it all greedily, and you love wealth with an intense love" (89:19–20). "Devouring it all greedily" translates "wa ta'kuloona" and "hubban jamma"; the reading and sense of these words are discussed here.

**Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 89, verses 21–23:**

Kalla idha ... wathaqahu ahad

"Dukkat al-ardu" (89:21): "the earth will be crushed." This means that its features will be obliterated and it will be leveled flat. This is one of the upheavals that will take place in this universe at the time the Resurrection occurs. As for the statement that the Lord (Rabb ta'ala) will descend in majesty and the angels will stand in rows, this is an unseen matter. We cannot understand its reality at this time, because we are still in this world and our power of perception is limited. However, this manner of expression brings to mind that the situation will be very awesome and terrifying. Similarly, the bringing of Hell is entirely beyond our understanding. However, it is clear that the wrongdoers will be brought near to it, and it will be brought near to the people of Hell. As for the actual condition and circumstances, that is an unseen matter, and it will become well known on that day when it comes to pass.

Through these verses, a scene is portrayed that makes hearts tremble. Eyes are cast down in fear. The pronunciation and rhythm of the words are also frightening, and the grip of the scenes is intense: the earth being reduced to dust, the Lord's descent in majesty and His issuing of judgments, the angels standing in ranks, and Hell being prepared and presented. These are scenes that cause fear to overtake a human being.

"Yawma'idhin yatadhakkaru al-insan" (89:23): "On that day, the human being will come to understand." That person will grasp the true reality, which in this world he was unable to grasp regarding the reality of wealth and poverty. He used to gather up all the inheritance wealth and consume it, and he would also usurp the rights of orphans and women. He was severely caught up in love of wealth. He neither honored the orphan nor made any effort for the livelihood of the needy. He was rebellious, and by the strength of his wealth and authority he would fill the earth with corruption. Such a person will understand everything today, and he will accept admonition well, but now the time has passed.

"Wa anna lahu al-dhikra" (89:23): "But what benefit will understanding be to him at that time?" The time for taking admonition and acting upon it has passed. What benefit will admonition give today? This is the abode of recompense. Now there is nothing but regret upon regret. For you, the abode of action was the life of this world, where you neither understood nor acted.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 89, verse 24:

He says: "Would that I had sent forward (something) for my life!" (89:24) Would that he had gathered some provision for the Hereafter by earning it. True life is that which can truly be called life. Preparations, earnings and storing up were necessary for this life. Oh, would that I had done something! This will be a sorrowful wish. And there, what will a person be able to do apart from these regretful wishes?

After these heart-rending regrets and futile wishes, now its outcome will be briefly this.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 89, verse 25–26:

﴿Then on that Day none will punish as He punishes,﴾ ﴿and none will bind as He binds.﴾ (89:25–26) Thus, on that Day, no one inflicts a punishment like the punishment of Allah, and no one binds as Allah binds. Allah is the All-Subduing, the Compeller. On that Day He will inflict a punishment for which there is no parallel, and the manner of His binding on that Day will also be such as cannot be imagined here. The Qur'an has described the scenes of Allah's seizing and His punishment many times and in a most captivating manner. Here it is simply stated that that punishment will be unique, that that seizing will also be unique, and that it will be such that there is no example of it in this world. And this situation stands in contrast to the scenes that this surah describes concerning the seizing of 'Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, their oppression, their tyranny and their mischief-making, how they seized people and did injustice. So, O Prophet and O believers, those people who have oppressed and have been persecuting and inflicting violence upon the Muslims here, or who are doing so, their condition in the Hereafter will be like this, and there is a difference like that between heaven and earth between the punishment and seizing of Allah and the punishment and seizing of creatures. The punishment and violence inflicted by worldly people are nothing compared with what these people are about to face. Therefore, let these people do whatever they wish, but know that their end will be very evil, far greater than our imagination.

In such terrifying scenes, in scenes of severe seizing and severe punishment, which we cannot even imagine, a call comes. This is addressed to the soul at peace (nafs mutma'innah), and it comes from the Exalted Assembly (Mala' A'la).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 89, verses 27–30:

ﷻ "Yaa ayyatuhan-nafsul-mutma'innah..." to "...jannati"

What an atmosphere of love, complete intimacy and nearness! O soul at peace, how much spirituality and how much honour and dignity there is in this call!

﴿Yaa ayyatuhan-nafsul-mutma'innah﴾ (89:27), "O soul at rest." Yet on the other side there is an unparalleled seizing and grabbing, an unparalleled and unimaginable punishment being inflicted, a harsh atmosphere. In this harsh atmosphere, this gentle and loving call!

﴿Irji'ii ila rabbiki﴾ (89:28), "Return to your Lord." Return to your true source, to your true cradle, which flows beneath the earth. Return now to your Lord. There is a special bond between you and your Lord, a special relationship, a special familiarity.

﴿Raadiyatam-mardiyyah﴾ (89:28), "You are pleased and Allah is pleased with you." By this joyful proclamation, the effusions of love and contentment spread over the atmosphere.

﴿Fadkhulii fii 'ibaadii﴾ (89:29), "Enter among My servants." Those who are My near and chosen servants, and may you too attain this nearness.

﴿Wadkhulii jannatii﴾ (89:30), "And enter My Paradise!" In My protection and in My mercy. In these verses, the love and tenderness are such that from the very beginning a breath of Paradise is felt.

From the words ﴿Yaa ayyatuhan-nafsul-mutma'innah﴾ (89:27), "O soul at rest," this breeze begins to blow. Which soul is this that is at rest? It is the soul at rest with its Lord, at rest and steadfast upon the path of truth, content with whatever befalls it on that path, content in prosperity and in poverty. It is content with the wealth of certainty, and therefore it does not abandon its path, nor does it stop tired and defeated on the road. It is content in this world and content amid the horrors of the Resurrection.

The atmosphere of the call in these verses is filled with the blessings and effusions of Allah in pleasure, contentment and tranquillity. The melody of the words and the fullness of meaning with nearness and serenity is the atmosphere of this call. This is the atmosphere of Paradise, and this atmosphere overflows and drips from the words and meanings of these verses. And upon it is the radiance of the manifestations of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
